# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](agent-data/prose.md#prose-form). It contains near term tasks with a
short description and uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

A cycle's record has one home at a time, and while the cycle runs this is it. At Preparation
the picked-up `## Todo` item **moves** here (never copied, one home per text) and becomes six
provisional items, all required, all revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block moves
into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and becomes that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in
two places. Shape:

```
### <type>: <title>

#### Problem
<what is wrong, a sentence or two>

#### Solution
<what will be done about it, broad; provisional until the close-out>

#### Acceptance check
<the measure of "are you finished?">

#### Ladder
- [[N]] [<cycle title> opening][M] (done)
- [[N]] [<title>][M] (current)
- [[N]] [<title>][M]
- [[N]] [<cycle title> closing][M]

#### Deliberation
<how the five above were decided; `_None._` if there was nothing to deliberate>

#### Ladder details
<one `#####` subsection per rung, closing included, headed by its exact title, opened at
laddering with the rung's intent and completed at landing with the conceptual delta, the
closing rung's at close-out with gotchas in problem/solution form>
```

A multi-cycle program adds one level: the program is the `###`, its current cycle the `####`,
and the six items sit one level below that (headings give the current work durable anchors,
which numbered Todo entries can't). Full rules in
[cycle-protocol.md](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#preparation); the move's four transforms are
in [Chores sections](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

### feat: measure reproducibility

#### Problem

Modern CPUs change their clock frequency continuously to save power. The OS's **power policy**
(the cpufreq governor plus, on AMD, the EPP hint) decides how eagerly the chip boosts under load
and how quickly it retreats, so the clock a run executes at depends on the box's recent history,
not its spec sheet. A latency number is cycles times cycle time, and the 2026-08-03 experiment
showed both failure shapes: under `powersave` the same code differed ~9% run to run as the clock
wandered, and a run parked on the un-boosted base clock graded A, flat being all the grade sees.
For A/B comparison the need is consistency, not speed: a stable clock at any rate beats an
unstable fast one. Today the harness cannot report the policy, cannot hold the clock still, and
no run's numbers survive the session that produced them, so a reader cannot tell a code delta
from a power-management delta. (Continues the cycle stalled since 2026-08-04.)

1	# custom-family.md - iiac-perf's layer, as a member of the vc-x1 agent-file family
2	
3	Read after [custom.md](custom.md), whose single convention entry points here. Present only in a
4	member repo: a project that is not a member does not carry this file, and nothing in it applies to
5	one.
6	
7	**A member's `custom.md` differs from the payload by that one line, and everything of its own lives
8	here.** That is the family's convention and it buys a property worth having: `diff custom.md
9	<template>/work/custom.md` is one line for every member, so the file that can never be pinned still
10	converges, and a member's whole customization surface is this file. The medium below is here for
11	that reason rather than because it has anything to do with the family.
12	
13	## Medium and validation
14	
15	The artifact is the `iiac-perf` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name
16	`iiac-perf`), with versioning specifics in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md).
17	
18	**What a version bump promises**: nothing to a dependent, because there are none. `iiac-perf` is
19	a binary crate with no library target and no external consumers, so `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to
20	readers of the history (see
21	[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)) and not a compatibility
22	contract. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.
23	
24	- **Full validation**
25	  - when: per-commit checklist step 5
26	  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
27	    1. `cargo fmt`
28	    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
29	    3. `cargo test`
30	    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
31	    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
32	- **Fast validation**
33	  - when: ladder checklist step 3
34	  - `cargo test --bins`
35	
36	The commands are the project's. The rule that each invocation's exit status is checked is
37	universal and lives in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#working-practices).
38	
39	## Membership
40	
41	- **member name**: `iiac-perf`
42	- **template repository**: `../vc-x1-template`
43	
44	These two are environment rather than instruction, the same species as `.vc-config.toml`'s
45	`[repos]` paths, and they belong there instead. They cannot move yet: `vc-x1 config --validate`
46	rejects keys it does not know (measured on 0.78.4, 2026-08-07), so a config carrying them would
47	fail its own validator.
48	
49	## Messaging
50	
51	Members notify each other through the `../vc-x1-messages` repo, one file per recipient, ours being
52	`../vc-x1-messages/iiac-perf.md`. The protocol is that repo's `README.md` and it governs. Message
53	bodies live in the sender's own repo (ours under `messages/`), and the messages repo holds only
54	pointer records. It replaced the template repository's mailboxes 2026-08-13, with the design
55	record in [chores-07](notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo). These are
56	the parts that decide how a session behaves.
57	
58	- **At acquaint, read `../vc-x1-messages/iiac-perf.md`.** Records sit newest first. A record with
59	  no `read` field is unread mail, and one with no `outcome-*` field is still open.
60	- **Mark, never delete.** Our file's persistence policy keeps every record: reading one adds a
61	  `read:` timestamp, and handling one adds `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` pointing at what
62	  came of it, usually a `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` section. The outcome closes the record, and
63	  the `read:` is what tells the sender it arrived.
64	- **Records are thin pointers, not state.** A record carries `local:` / `remote:` references to
65	  the body, so anything worth keeping is already a committed file in the sender's repo, and the
66	  old copy-before-delete step (learned 2026-08-05) is obsolete.
67	- **Whoever writes a record commits it**, in the messages repo. Write to a member's file there,
68	  never into their repo: a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent.
69	- **Durable mail is push-then-record.** A `remote:` field is a commit permalink, so the body's
70	  commit pushes before the record naming it is written. Local-only records are fine for same-day
71	  traffic between siblings.
72	
73	## Dogfood log
74	
75	Dated entries on what this project is trying and where the pinned instructions chafed, failed, or
76	got amended: the evidence base for the family's convergence decisions
77	([Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
78	
79	Each entry carries a **status**: `proposed` (in our agent-files, awaiting the family),
80	`adopted family-wide`, `rejected`, or `permanently local`. In-flight entries only: on
81	resolution an entry retires to [done.md](notes/done.md) with its narrative in
82	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, adopted and rejected alike. Entries predating the status
83	convention keep their form until touched.
84	
85	- 2026-08-14 (`proposed`): the semicolon allowance goes, and the agent-files sweep to zero
86	  - the pinned rule blessed the "between equals" join and left everything else a judgment call.
87	    wink's observation: agents take advantage of the exceptions, so the allowance is claimed
88	    wherever a semicolon is wanted
89	  - the rule is now flat: prose carries no semicolons, and a semicolon appears only in code
90	    (code spans, fenced code, source files), where it is syntax. Each prose site converts to a
91	    period, a comma with a conjunction, or sub-bullets
92	  - the agent-files (custom* included) carry no historical exemption and sweep to zero. Any
93	    other historical file keeps its semicolons only until altered, and altering one means
94	    asking the user whether they should go (wink, tightened mid-rung from a silent
95	    convert-when-touched). Excluding src/'s ~125 existing comment-line joins from this cycle's
96	    sweep is wink's call, keeping it focused on agent-file convergence
97	  - the rule tightened is one vc-x1 wrote and swept at ~140 sites. Proposed to them by message
98	    after this cycle lands, with their own instruction back: review the rule, not each instance
99	  - rationale in
100	    [chores-07](notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-semicolons-leave-the-agent-files)
101	
102	- 2026-08-12 (`proposed`): validation runs at every commit, and the notes-only skip goes
103	  - the per-commit checklist stamped the version-of-record at step 4 and let step 5 be skipped
104	    for notes-only commits, so a commit could carry a version that no build ever had. Measured
105	    the same day: 0.24.5 and 0.24.6 both stamped and neither built, and `-V` answered 0.24.4
106	    until the next close-out jumped it three
107	  - wink's rule and his reason: every commit bumps the version precisely so a build exists
108	    carrying it, which makes an unbuilt bump a version nobody can run and the banner a claim
109	    nobody checked
110	  - so the skip goes at all three sites, and the step is conditioned on the medium rather than on

112	    escape "too costly to build", which asks every project to judge its own cost and would be

118	    cycle-at-a-glance clause that named validation as a close-out specialty. The stale number is
119	    the argument in miniature: it was a restatement, which is what let it drift unnoticed
120	  - rationale in [chores-06](notes/chores/chores-06.md#docs-validate-every-commit)
121	
122	- 2026-08-07 (`proposed`): the family layer splits out of `custom.md`
123	  - `custom.md` had been accumulating things that only make sense because this repo belongs to a
124	    family: a member name, a template path, and a dogfood log whose status vocabulary reads
125	    `adopted family-wide`. wink's test is that `custom.md` should be usable as-is by a project that
126	    has never heard of us, and it failed that test
127	  - so the family layer moves here, and `custom.md` shrinks to a stub with nothing to substitute:
128	    a title naming no project, and one section. A member's copy differs from the payload's by the
129	    single conventions entry that points here, so `diff custom.md <template>/work/custom.md` is one
130	    line for every member
131	  - the pointer is that entry rather than an intro sentence (wink). We argued for the intro, on the
132	    grounds that four members carrying an identical one-line diff looks like a fake divergence.
133	    The answer is that it is a real project convention, and one line is cheaper than a paragraph

135	  - the chain is `AGENTS.md` -> `custom.md` -> here, all of it prose, which is what lets the pinned
136	    set stay ignorant of the split. A non-member has no entry and no file
137	  - `CLAUDE.md` collapses to one line, `@AGENTS.md` (wink). It had grown a second `@` import per
138	    layer, which made it a second statement of what to read and therefore a second thing to keep
139	    true. Now `AGENTS.md` is the only source of that truth, and `CLAUDE.md` is payload-identical for

141	    auto-loaded any more, so hard rule 0 is load-bearing rather than a formality
142	  - one consequence needs the family's agreement, not ours: **"Check the mailbox at acquaint" leaves
143	    the pinned `AGENTS.md`** and lands in `## Messaging` above. vc-x1 pinned it in the 20260802
144	    snapshot, so this is a reversal. The argument is that a non-member cannot perform it at all,
145	    since building the mailbox path needs a member name and a template path they do not have, so it
146	    is dead text naming concepts they lack rather than a harmless no-op
147	  - deliberately not opened in the same pass: `AGENTS.md` still says "the family" and "member" where

149	    up, and folding it in would roughly double the review surface of an already large configuration

151	- 2026-08-07 (`proposed`): cycles run on a bookmark, and `custom.md` stops holding rules

member repo: a project that is not a member does not carry this file, and nothing in it applies to
one.

**A member's `custom.md` differs from the payload by that one line, and everything of its own lives
here.** That is the family's convention and it buys a property worth having: `diff custom.md
<template>/work/custom.md` is one line for every member, so the file that can never be pinned still
converges, and a member's whole customization surface is this file. The medium below is here for
that reason rather than because it has anything to do with the family.

## Medium and validation

The artifact is the `iiac-perf` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name
`iiac-perf`), with versioning specifics in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md).

**What a version bump promises**: nothing to a dependent, because there are none. `iiac-perf` is
a binary crate with no library target and no external consumers, so `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to
readers of the history (see
[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)) and not a compatibility
contract. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.

- **Full validation**
  - when: per-commit checklist step 5
  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
    1. `cargo fmt`
    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
    3. `cargo test`
    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
- **Fast validation**
  - when: ladder checklist step 3
  - `cargo test --bins`

The commands are the project's. The rule that each invocation's exit status is checked is
universal and lives in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#working-practices).

## Membership

- **member name**: `iiac-perf`
- **template repository**: `../vc-x1-template`

These two are environment rather than instruction, the same species as `.vc-config.toml`'s
`[repos]` paths, and they belong there instead. They cannot move yet: `vc-x1 config --validate`
rejects keys it does not know (measured on 0.78.4, 2026-08-07), so a config carrying them would
fail its own validator.

## Messaging

Members notify each other through the `../vc-x1-messages` repo, one file per recipient, ours being
`../vc-x1-messages/iiac-perf.md`. The protocol is that repo's `README.md` and it governs. Message
bodies live in the sender's own repo (ours under `messages/`), and the messages repo holds only
pointer records. It replaced the template repository's mailboxes 2026-08-13, with the design
record in [chores-07](notes/chores/chores-07.md#docs-design-the-vc-x1-messages-repo). These are
the parts that decide how a session behaves.

- **At acquaint, read `../vc-x1-messages/iiac-perf.md`.** Records sit newest first. A record with
  no `read` field is unread mail, and one with no `outcome-*` field is still open.
- **Mark, never delete.** Our file's persistence policy keeps every record: reading one adds a
  `read:` timestamp, and handling one adds `outcome-local:` / `outcome-remote:` pointing at what
  came of it, usually a `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` section. The outcome closes the record, and
  the `read:` is what tells the sender it arrived.
- **Records are thin pointers, not state.** A record carries `local:` / `remote:` references to
  the body, so anything worth keeping is already a committed file in the sender's repo, and the
  old copy-before-delete step (learned 2026-08-05) is obsolete.
- **Whoever writes a record commits it**, in the messages repo. Write to a member's file there,
  never into their repo: a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent.
- **Durable mail is push-then-record.** A `remote:` field is a commit permalink, so the body's
  commit pushes before the record naming it is written. Local-only records are fine for same-day
  traffic between siblings.

##### feat: read, pin, and restore the CPU frequency

For comparison the need is consistency, not speed (wink, 2026-08-15): a stable clock at any rate
beats an unstable fast one, so the harness gains the ability to hold the clock still and the
user gains commands to check, set, and unset that state at any time.

- three command words: `read-freq` prints the clock state (governor, EPP, min/max, boost,
  current frequency, per policy group), `pin-freq` holds the clock at one frequency (min = max,
  boost off), and `restore-freq` converges the box to the user's declared steady state
- **the default pin target is load-independent** (wink, 2026-08-15): with no frequency
  configured or given, `pin-freq` pins at base clock, the manufacturer's guaranteed frequency
  under sustained all-core load, so the unconfigured pin works for every bench as it stands
  today. Any faster "best" is workload- and schedule-dependent (thermal), and picking one is a
  measurement, not a default
  - discovery order: `acpi_cppc/nominal_freq` (reads 3801 MHz on the 3900x, the 3.8 GHz base
    clock matching the measured 3.7929 GHz TSC rate), then intel_pstate's `base_frequency`,
    else the highest non-boost frequency the driver lists. We think that last fallback covers
    the Pi, to be verified at implementation. `read-freq` prints what it resolved and from
    where
- a declared or given pin value is validated against the box at pin time, never in the
  abstract: the valid range is sysfs's per-policy `cpuinfo_min_freq`..`cpuinfo_max_freq`
  (discrete `scaling_available_frequencies` on drivers that list them), a bad value errors
  naming that range, and `read-freq` prints the range so the user picks informed
- **the restore target is declared, not remembered** (wink, 2026-08-15): the user's preferred
  steady state lives in the layered config's markdown carrier (a `[freq]` section, normally in
  the XDG file `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md`, since the steady state is the box's, not the
  project's), written once by the user, beside prose saying what it means
  - why not save-and-restore-what-we-found: transient state files are a demonstrated failure
    mode in this repo, and restoring the displaced state ratchets on back-to-back runs. Run 2
    enters while run 1's pin is live, "restores" the pin, and a laptop or a phone is left
    pinned high. Convergence to a declared state is idempotent from any starting point

  terminal prompt, a GUI panel beside the time-of-day): one short line, fast, stable format

  than half-working

  panic, SIGINT/SIGTERM. The uncatchable paths (SIGKILL, power loss) need no saved state to
  recover from: `restore-freq` converges from anywhere, any time

  throttling is unlikely to reach below base

  verifiable from its record

1	# Cycle checklists
2	
3	Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
4	protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
5	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md). On any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
6	the relevant checklist immediately before the action. Don't run it from memory.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## The cycle at a glance
13	
14	Every change runs as a **cycle** with three phases: Preparation -> Work -> Close-out. The
15	phases always happen, but there are two styles. A **multi-step** cycle commits them
16	individually, as a ladder of steps (the Preparation commit is optional). A
17	**single-step** cycle folds all three into one commit when the change is straightforward, so
18	that one commit is the close-out and carries its duties. So a
19	single-step cycle is one commit, and a multi-step is minimum two (a Work commit plus the
20	close-out), typically three or more (the definition is
21	[AGENTS.md's Terminology](../AGENTS.md#terminology)). The
22	ladder lists a cycle's steps in order and identifies each by its title, with no number and no
23	version. Where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
24	[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md) before any commit
25	work, and before any push, cycle or not.
26	
27	## Cycles run on a bookmark
28	
29	A cycle runs on one topic bookmark in the work repo, created at the opening and named by the
30	cycle title's slug (the anchor algorithm in
31	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). `main` advances only when the
32	finished cycle lands on it, and nothing pushes straight to `main`. The bot repo needs no bookmark:
33	its `main` rides the tip of its linear narrative.
34	
35	- **The bookmark is the unit of review.** Everything the cycle does is visible as one line
36	  against `main`, and until it lands the whole line is a draft that can be reshaped
37	  ([Topic bookmarks are drafts](#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)). Landing is the single approval
38	  that makes the cycle permanent.
39	- **Create at the opening**, land at the close-out. Commands are in
40	  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), and the opening's other duties are in
41	  the [Opening checklist](#opening-checklist) below.
42	- **A single-step cycle still gets one.** The saving is not worth the exception, and a
43	  one-commit line is exactly the case where a pre-landing rewrite is cheapest.
44	- **The permanent branch is whatever this project calls it** (`main` here). A long-lived program
45	  bookmark is a different animal, governed by
46	  [Long-lived bookmarks](jj.md#long-lived-bookmarks-merge-only-by-default-deletable-once-merged).
47	
48	**Why:** a cycle that pushes `main` directly makes every correction a coordinated force-push of
49	published history. Landing costs one command and buys free rewrites for the whole cycle.
50	
51	## Opening checklist
52	
53	At the cycle's opening, before the first Work commit:
54	
55	1. Create the cycle's bookmark ([Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
56	2. Move the picked-up item into `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and write the **six provisional
57	   items** there, all six required. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
58	   own level, and the other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###`
59	   title, `####` items, and under a program heading, each one deeper):
60	   - **title**, which becomes the chores section header at close-out
61	   - **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
62	   - **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad
63	   - **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?"
64	   - **ladder**: one rung per step, `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` plus `(current)` / `(done)`, with
65	     `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References`. The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`,
66	     is linked like the rest
67	   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
68	     deliberate)
69	   A `Ladder details` area follows the six: one subsection per rung, closing included, headed
70	   by the rung's exact title, opened at laddering with the rung's intent and completed as rungs
71	   land, the closing rung's at close-out (see the protocol's
72	   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)).
73	3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
74	   version-of-record.
75	
76	Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
77	moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).
78	
79	**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
80	of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
81	against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
82	sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
83	the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
84	done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
85	same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.
86	
87	## Committing vs pushing
88	
89	A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
90	commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
91	`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
92	pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
93	an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
94	is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
95	publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
96	around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
97	cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).
98	
99	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
100	
101	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
102	So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
103	the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.
104	
105	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
106	  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
107	  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
108	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
109	- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**:
110	  - the bookmark has already landed
111	  - another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase
112	  - the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees
113	
114	The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
115	multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
116	[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
117	
118	## Per-commit checklist
119	
120	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
121	[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):
122	
123	1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
124	2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
125	3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit, and complete the rung's
126	   `Ladder details` subsection with the conceptual delta (its intent stub was opened when the
127	   rung was laddered, and the ladder itself stays a bare ToC). See the protocol's
128	   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation).
129	4. Bump the version-of-record to this commit's version (the suffix scheme is in
130	   [versioning.md](versioning.md)). The opening checklist's bump already covers a Preparation
131	   commit.
132	5. Validate the artifact at every commit, doc-only ones included. The medium's commands are in
133	   [custom.md](../custom.md).
134	6. Stop and ask the user, "please review", as this is the bottom of the review loop. Do not present
135	   a description as we iterate until the user reviews and says "continue|go|.." indicating the work
136	   review is likely complete.
137	7. Once the work review is complete, write the description: a conventional title, then a body in
138	   prose.md's [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form) (an intro paragraph stating the
139	   general problem, `*` bullets for its facets, `-` bullets for solutions, a `-` solving the
140	   nearest enclosing problem), sized per [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths). No version in
141	   either, no file list (the diff is the mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo,
142	   and the session hold that). See [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
143	8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
144	   explicitly includes it.
145	9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
146	   `jj commit`. Never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.
147	
148	## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist
149	
150	Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
151	[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):
152	
153	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
154	2. Do the commit's work.
155	3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
156	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
157	   the one permitted describe. The commit is never published and never carries a trailer.
158	
159	Nothing on a ladder is pushed. The close-out squash
160	(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
161	publishes the single commit.
162

# Cycle checklists

Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md). On any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
the relevant checklist immediately before the action. Don't run it from memory.

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## The cycle at a glance

Every change runs as a **cycle** with three phases: Preparation -> Work -> Close-out. The
phases always happen, but there are two styles. A **multi-step** cycle commits them
individually, as a ladder of steps (the Preparation commit is optional). A
**single-step** cycle folds all three into one commit when the change is straightforward, so
that one commit is the close-out and carries its duties. So a
single-step cycle is one commit, and a multi-step is minimum two (a Work commit plus the
close-out), typically three or more (the definition is
[AGENTS.md's Terminology](../AGENTS.md#terminology)). The
ladder lists a cycle's steps in order and identifies each by its title, with no number and no
version. Where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md) before any commit
work, and before any push, cycle or not.

## Cycles run on a bookmark

A cycle runs on one topic bookmark in the work repo, created at the opening and named by the
cycle title's slug (the anchor algorithm in
[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). `main` advances only when the
finished cycle lands on it, and nothing pushes straight to `main`. The bot repo needs no bookmark:
its `main` rides the tip of its linear narrative.

- **The bookmark is the unit of review.** Everything the cycle does is visible as one line
  against `main`, and until it lands the whole line is a draft that can be reshaped
  ([Topic bookmarks are drafts](#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)). Landing is the single approval
  that makes the cycle permanent.
- **Create at the opening**, land at the close-out. Commands are in
  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), and the opening's other duties are in
  the [Opening checklist](#opening-checklist) below.
- **A single-step cycle still gets one.** The saving is not worth the exception, and a
  one-commit line is exactly the case where a pre-landing rewrite is cheapest.
- **The permanent branch is whatever this project calls it** (`main` here). A long-lived program
  bookmark is a different animal, governed by
  [Long-lived bookmarks](jj.md#long-lived-bookmarks-merge-only-by-default-deletable-once-merged).

**Why:** a cycle that pushes `main` directly makes every correction a coordinated force-push of
published history. Landing costs one command and buys free rewrites for the whole cycle.

## Opening checklist

At the cycle's opening, before the first Work commit:

1. Create the cycle's bookmark ([Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
2. Move the picked-up item into `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and write the **six provisional
   items** there, all six required. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
   own level, and the other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###`
   title, `####` items, and under a program heading, each one deeper):
   - **title**, which becomes the chores section header at close-out
   - **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
   - **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad
   - **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?"
   - **ladder**: one rung per step, `- [[N]] [<title>][M]` plus `(current)` / `(done)`, with
     `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References`. The closing rung, `<cycle title> closing`,
     is linked like the rest
   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
     deliberate)
   A `Ladder details` area follows the six: one subsection per rung, closing included, headed
   by the rung's exact title, opened at laddering with the rung's intent and completed as rungs
   land, the closing rung's at close-out (see the protocol's
   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)).
3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
   version-of-record.

Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.

## Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Topic bookmarks are drafts

A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**:
  - the bookmark has already landed
  - another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase
  - the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees

The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit, and complete the rung's
   `Ladder details` subsection with the conceptual delta (its intent stub was opened when the
   rung was laddered, and the ladder itself stays a bare ToC). See the protocol's
   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation).
4. Bump the version-of-record to this commit's version (the suffix scheme is in
   [versioning.md](versioning.md)). The opening checklist's bump already covers a Preparation
   commit.
5. Validate the artifact at every commit, doc-only ones included. The medium's commands are in
   [custom.md](../custom.md).
6. Stop and ask the user, "please review", as this is the bottom of the review loop. Do not present
   a description as we iterate until the user reviews and says "continue|go|.." indicating the work
   review is likely complete.
7. Once the work review is complete, write the description: a conventional title, then a body in
   prose.md's [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form) (an intro paragraph stating the
   general problem, `*` bullets for its facets, `-` bullets for solutions, a `-` solving the
   nearest enclosing problem), sized per [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths). No version in
   either, no file list (the diff is the mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo,
   and the session hold that). See [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`. Never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe. The commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed. The close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval. "Commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
  bounded task only. Delegation waives stops, never flow (records, validation, the bookmark
  discipline, per the protocol's [Policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy)), and destructive ops
  still pause.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are already written. Nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no

push. See
[After push or squash-push](cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

The cycle's last step, per the protocol's

1. **Run the acceptance check** the opening stated, and record what it showed in the
   `## In Progress` block, whether or not it passed. A check that was never run is a failed
   close-out, and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to quietly restate the banner.
2. **Finalize the six items in place**: sync the title if the scope shifted, replace the
   provisional solution statement with what was done, drop the ladder's `(current)` / `(done)`
   markers, add any design subsections, and complete the closing rung's subsection: gotchas in
   problem/solution form, `_None._` when closing surfaced none.
3. **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, which is what creates the section.

   into the destination's namespace, repo-root-relative links gain `../`, forward-looking notes

4. Write the `## Done` entry: the version, then a bold title line with its chores `[N]` ref,

5. Full validation, mandatory.
6. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
7. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for

   [in the protocol](cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe). Its step 4 is

The user question first, then my read of the code. I looked at what vc-x1 actually has and how it's wired.

**What's shareable is smaller than it looks.** The genuinely generic piece is `md_fence.rs` alone: 81 lines, deliberately std-only with zero crate dependencies, because vc-x1's `build.rs` pulls it in via `#[path]` as a second crate. `config_md.rs` (255 lines) is not shareable as-is: it hard-codes vc-x1's filenames (`.vc-config.md`), their flat `toml_simple` string-map parser, and their workspace topology. Our loader is typed serde with `deny_unknown_fields`, so our resolver half will be different code no matter what.

**On the lib-module-then-package path, I agree with the destination but would skip the middle step.** Three levels of commitment exist:

1. **Copy the 81-line filter** (what the ladder rung already specs). Cheap, no coordination, and the duplication surface is one small, stable, test-covered function.
2. **Lib target in vc-x1 + path dependency from us.** This is the step I'd argue against: vc-x1 is currently bin-only (package name `vc-x1-dev`), a path dep couples our build to a sibling checkout (`cargo install --path . --locked` then fails on any box without `../vc-x1`), and it ties our validation to their refactors mid-flight.

# iiac-perf configuration — sample showing every key at its
# built-in default.
#
# Copy to one of (nearer file wins, field by field):
#   $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/iiac-perf/config.toml   per-user; ~/.config/
#                                            iiac-perf/config.toml if
#                                            XDG_CONFIG_HOME is unset
#   ./iiac-perf.toml                         project-local, current
#                                            directory only (no
#                                            upward walk)
#
# Precedence, lowest to highest:
#   built-in defaults < XDG file < project-local file < CLI flags
#
# Every key is optional; an omitted key keeps the built-in default
# shown here. A present-but-malformed file is a hard error (a typo
# surfaces rather than silently reverting to defaults). The startup
# banner's `config` line names the files that were loaded.

# Target wall-clock seconds per bench — the `-d` / `--duration`
# default. Any positive number. `-d` on the CLI overrides it; `-D`
# (total budget split per bench) also overrides it.
duration = 5.0

# Histogram band-label style — the `--band-labels` default. One of:
#   "zpn"  nines/zeros + decile names        (z3, p50, n4)
#   "frac" literal boundary fractions        (0.001, 0.50, 0.999_9)
#   "both" zpn and fraction side by side     (teaches the vocabulary)
band_labels = "both"

# Decimal digits on the report's time columns — the `--decimals`
# default. Integer 0 to 3:
#   0  integer nanoseconds
#   1  sub-ns precision that picosecond recording captures
#   3  the recording floor (more digits would be artifacts)
decimals = 1

# Seconds the first bench of a process spends warming the box
# before it records anything — the `--settle-time` default. Zero or
# more; 0 skips the warm. Paid once per process: the boost it wins
# is machine state, which every later bench inherits. Without it
# the first bench of a process reports a cold machine's numbers
# (~8.6% slow on a 7600x). The report's `env warmup:` row says how
# long the box actually took to settle.
settle_time = 1.5

# `--warm-cap` default. Zero or more; 0 caps immediately, which
# measures what the warm is worth. Every run warms until the
# trailing probe window grades A (and the delivered clock holds
# still, where readable) or until this cap; a settled box exits in
# ~50 ms, so the cap prices only the disturbed case. Hitting it is
# reported in the grade block, never silently absorbed.

content.text:
The quickest path is the same one I used for the smoke run: point `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` at a scratch dir so you don't touch your real `~/.config`, and give it an `.md` config whose fences carry the settings.

```sh
mkdir -p tmp/xdg/iiac-perf
cat > tmp/xdg/iiac-perf/config.md <<'EOF'
# my test config

Keep runs short while testing.

```toml
duration = 0.2
```

Pin profiles for the 3900x.

```toml
[profiles]
smt = "0,12"
```
EOF

XDG_CONFIG_HOME=$PWD/tmp/xdg iiac-perf min-now --settle-time 0
```

Three things to look for in the output:

1. The banner's `config` line names `.../tmp/xdg/iiac-perf/config.md`.
2. The bench header reads `duration=0.2s`, proving the fenced TOML was parsed (drop `duration` from the file and it goes back to the 5.0 default).
3. `--pin smt` expands the profile from the markdown file.

To see the both-carriers error:

```sh
echo 'duration = 0.3' > tmp/xdg/iiac-perf/config.toml
XDG_CONFIG_HOME=$PWD/tmp/xdg iiac-perf min-now --settle-time 0
```

It refuses at startup, naming both paths, before spending any time measuring. Remove either file and it runs again.

For the project-local carrier instead, `cd` into any scratch directory, write the same content as `iiac-perf.md` there, and run without the env var — the lookup is current-directory only, no upward walk. And prose is genuinely inert: type `duration = 99` in a prose line or an untagged fence and it changes nothing.

When you're done, `rm -r tmp/xdg` cleans up.

Raising settle-time to 5 s pushed total spin past the threshold, so the drop landed mid-measurement — and the grade correctly went F where the 2026-08-03 harness would have printed a clean-looking number.

The trace answers both halves of your question, and it caught something subtler than the last run. Here's the full picture from the record:

```
5.1-5.9s  cpu1/cpu13   4.51-4.54 GHz   (bench starts near max boost)
6.0s      -> cpu12     3.62 GHz        (one sample mid-transition)
6.0-9.4s  cpu12/cpu0   4.07-4.09 GHz   (the sustained state)
9.5-10s   cpu0/cpu12   4.37-4.54 GHz   (wanders back up at the end)
```

**On the settle cell**: it's not the exit-instant clock. `settle_s = 0.01` says the earliest warmup suffix that grades A with a stable clock starts 0.01 s in, and the `@4.09GHz` is the **median delivered clock across that settled suffix** — essentially the whole 5 s warmup. It's a median by design, so one odd read can't name the state. So it does describe warmup's sustained condition, end included, but this run shows why it can't be read as "the bench's starting clock": warmup certified 4.09, and the bench's first second promptly ran at 4.54 on a different core. Both cells are truthful; the box changed state at the boundary. That exact shape is what the settle fix was built to expose.

**On 4.09 being "slow"**: the 3900X is 3.8 GHz base, 4.6 GHz max boost — but 4.6 is opportunistic and single-core-short-burst. The trace shows the box *can* deliver 4.54 and did, in stretches, but under sustained spin with `powersave`/`balance_performance` the governor parks at ~4.09, a boost state above base but well under peak. So the machine is ramping; it just won't hold the top state, and it changes its mind mid-run.

**The core correlation is suggestive**: the 4.54 stretch ran on cpu1/cpu13 (SMT siblings of one physical core), the drop to 4.07-4.09 coincided with migration to cpu12/cpu0 (siblings of another), and the lone 3.62 sample — below base — is the transition moment itself. We think this is amd-pstate's preferred-core ranking plus per-core boost budgets, but the late 4.52 stretch on the *same* cpu0 says it isn't purely per-core, so that's speculation, not measurement.

Note also the run-to-run difference: your previous run fell to the base-clock 24.0 ns cluster; this one never sustained base at all, wandering 4.5 -> 4.1 -> 4.5. Same command, same box, different clock story each time — which is the whole cycle's thesis, and why `pin-freq` (min = max at base clock, boost off) is the next-but-one rung: a pinned trace is a flat line with nothing to wander between, verifiable from exactly this record (min = max in `clock_khz`).

The plain version: the settle number is warmup's typical speed, not the speed at the moment measuring began. Your chip's headline 4.6 GHz is a sprint it only does in bursts; left to its own power policy it cruised at 4.1, occasionally surging to 4.5, and switched between those mid-measurement — the report and the record now catch it doing that in the act.
